Source for this is the Alternative Hypothesis Reader, I can post a link if anyone cares. I plan to post more things from that reader in the future, some fascinating stuff in there.

Four different experiments were done to see how often fake science papers make it into peer reviewed journals

1) In 2005, some programmers created a program that randomly generated science papers, called SCIgen. They submitted to the 2005 World Multiconference on Systemics, Cybernetics and Informatics. They were invited to speak there, and exposed the hoax rather than actually discuss the paper itself. Another scientist, Dominique Labbe, combed through two other journals after this happened and some submission experiment was undertaken, and found that one journal had an acceptance rate of 13.3% of fake SCIgen papers, and another had 28%. For Springer journals, so far 16 have been found.

2) John Bohannon wrote a fake paper and made 304 slightly different copies, using google translate to make the English a bit disjointed. They were all sent to 304 different journals. Of the reputable journals he sent the papers to and for which he got results (so not including the pending ones), 44.4% were rejected without peer review, 11.1% were rejected with peer review, 24.3% were accepted without peer review, and 20.1% were accepted with peer review. Those are from journals considered to be in good standing, professional, and reputable.

3) Fiona Godlee performed an experiment like this in 1998. She took a paper about to be published in British Medical Journal, changed it to have 8 major errors, and sent it to 420 reviewers, only 221 of which returned it. Of those 221, 35 of them found no errors at all, and no reviewer found more than 5 major errors. The median number of errors found was 2.

4) In 1997, from the paper “Who Reviews the Reviewers? Feasibility of Using a Fictitious Manuscript to Evaluate Peer Reviewer Performance”, the authors sent an intentionally bad manuscript to all of the reviewers at Annals of Emergency Medicine. At the time of submission, the journal had an acceptance rate of 26%. Of the 262 reviewers this paper was sent to, 63 gave no response, 117 rejected it, 67 revised and returned it, and 15 accepted it immediately.
